passage: The scholarship form closed on Friday, and Rashmi's hands were damp on the mouse. Name, father's name, date of birth, marks. She spread her school ID and birth certificate beside the laptop and read each field twice against them. Halfway down she froze: she had typed "Sharama" but the certificate said "Sharma". She fixed it, then saved a draft instead of pressing submit. The next morning she carried a printout to Salma ma'am and asked, "Can you check before I send it?" The teacher spotted that the income certificate was missing from the uploads. Rashmi found the paper at home, scanned it, and submitted with a whole day to spare. The confirmation page showed her name, spelled right.

qa.q: What did Rashmi spread beside the laptop?
qa.a: She spread her school ID and birth certificate beside the laptop.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when she froze over the surname?
qa.a: Anxious, worried that one wrong letter would be hard to fix after submitting.

qa.q: Why was saving a draft and asking the teacher a good move?
qa.a: It gave time to have the form checked, and Salma ma'am spotted the missing income certificate before it became a mistake that was hard to correct.

qa.q: How might Salma ma'am have seen Rashmi's request to check before sending?
qa.a: Salma probably saw a careful student and was glad to be asked early, since the teacher caught the missing income certificate in time.

grounding: Shows a teenager anxious over spelling and documents on a scholarship form, checking against ID and asking before submitting.

passage:
"Ammi, the form wants my name exactly as on the marksheet."
"So type it."
"The marksheet says Dilnaaz with two a's, and my ID says Dilnaz. Which one do I use?"
Rehana put on her glasses. "Show me both." She looked from one card to the other. "Don't guess. If it goes wrong, it's hard to fix later."
"My stomach hurts, Ammi. I'll just press submit and hope."
"No. Save the draft. Tomorrow I'll come with you to the school office and ask which one the board wants."
"Really?"
"Really. Write your questions down tonight."
Dilnaz saved the draft and listed three questions in her notebook. The next day the clerk at the school office showed her the board's rule: use the marksheet spelling.

qa.q: How does the name on Dilnaz's marksheet differ from her ID?
qa.a: The marksheet says Dilnaaz with two a's, and her ID says Dilnaz.

qa.q: What is Dilnaz feeling when she says her stomach hurts?
qa.a: Anxious and afraid of making a mistake on the form, so much that she is tempted to press submit and hope.

qa.q: What turning point stopped Dilnaz from a risky click?
qa.a: Rehana told her not to guess, so Dilnaz saved the draft and planned to ask at the school office.

qa.q: What does Rehana's offer to come to the school office suggest about how she sees Dilnaz's worry?
qa.a: Rehana takes the worry seriously and wants to support Dilnaz, staying calm and guiding her to ask rather than guess.

grounding: Shows a teenager anxious about a name mismatch on an exam form, checking documents and asking before submitting.

passage:
Monday. Nitin opened the board exam form on the school computer. He typed fast: name, father's name, date of birth. At the end the screen showed "NITHIN KUMAR." His ID said "NITIN KUMAR." His stomach dropped. The submit button was right there.
Wednesday. He hadn't slept well. He went to Yogesh sir in the staff room. "Sir, one letter is wrong. Will they reject my exam?" Yogesh sir said, "It's still a draft. Don't submit anything. Bring your ID and the birth certificate."
Friday. They sat side by side. Nitin read each line aloud against his ID: spelling, date, parents' names, photo size. He found a second mistake, the pin code. Yogesh sir only pointed at the "Preview" button. Nitin corrected both, checked once more, and then clicked submit. He printed the confirmation page and kept it in a plastic folder.

qa.q: What name did the screen show at the end?
qa.a: The screen showed "NITHIN KUMAR."

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling on Wednesday, and what shows it?
qa.a: Nitin was anxious that the exam would be rejected; he hadn't slept well and went to ask Yogesh sir about one wrong letter.

qa.q: Which step on Friday is worth copying for any form?
qa.a: Reading each line aloud against the ID before submitting, because it caught a second mistake, the pin code.

qa.q: How might Yogesh sir see Nitin's worry?
qa.a: Yogesh sir takes it seriously but stays calm, treating the mistake as fixable because the form is still a draft.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager anxious about a spelling mistake in an exam form who checks every line against his ID and asks before submitting.

passage:
Sit, Hemant. You want to rush that scholarship form tonight? Let your Nilesh kaka tell you something first.
When I was in Class Ten, there was a merit scholarship from the district. I filled the form in one sitting at the post office counter, pen borrowed from the clerk. I wrote my birth year wrong. One digit. I didn't read it back. The headmaster signed it without reading either.
Three months later the list came, and my name was missing. The office said my age didn't match my school record. My mother walked with me to the district office four times. Each time, a new affidavit, a new stamp. By the time it was fixed, that year's money was gone.
Next year I filled it again. This time I sat at home, read every line against my school certificate, and asked the headmaster to check before I posted it. I got it. Now, beta, show me your form.

qa.q: Where did Nilesh fill the form the first time?
qa.a: Nilesh filled the form in one sitting at the post office counter.

qa.q: What was young Nilesh feeling when the list came without Nilesh's name?
qa.a: Nilesh must have felt shocked and ashamed, since one careless digit had cost the scholarship.

qa.q: What choice in the story would have prevented the mistake?
qa.a: Reading the form back against the school certificate before handing it in, as Nilesh did the second year.

qa.q: How might Nilesh's mother have felt walking to the district office four times?
qa.a: She was probably tired and worried but determined, standing by Nilesh through every new affidavit and stamp.

grounding: An elder recalls how one unchecked digit on a scholarship form cost a year, and how careful checking and asking first fixed it.

passage:
The scholarship portal closed at five. At twenty past three the cyber café lost power.
Shankar stood outside with his file, heart thumping. His sister Bhavna had taken the afternoon off from the tailoring shop to come with him. "The generator will start," she said, not very sure.
It started at four. The café was loud with a cricket match on someone's phone. Shankar typed his name and clicked on the upload box for the income certificate, and then froze. The certificate said "Sankar." The ID said "Shankar."
"Just upload it," the café boy said. "Nobody checks."
Bhavna called the helpline number printed on the notice instead. The line was busy twice. On the third try a woman told them to upload both documents plus a signed note explaining the spelling. Shankar wrote it by hand, Bhavna photographed it, and he read every field aloud before clicking submit at 4:48.

qa.q: At what time did Shankar click submit?
qa.a: He clicked submit at 4:48.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling when he noticed the spelling on the certificate?
qa.a: Shankar was anxious and frozen with worry, because the two spellings did not match and time was running out.

qa.q: Which choice worked better than the café boy's advice, and why?
qa.a: Calling the helpline to ask before submitting worked better, because it gave a proper fix instead of risking a rejected form.

qa.q: How does Bhavna see the afternoon?
qa.a: Bhavna treats it as important enough to leave work for, and she stays calm and practical by calling the helpline.

grounding: Shows a teenager under time pressure who notices a spelling mismatch and asks officials before submitting rather than guessing.

passage: The science olympiad form had a red warning in capitals: DETAILS CANNOT BE CHANGED AFTER SUBMISSION. Arohi read it three times at the dining table of the Salt Lake flat, and her stomach knotted. Name: she typed it, deleted it, typed it again slowly, then held her school ID card beside the screen and checked every letter. Date of birth: the form wanted the month first. Her birth certificate said 07/03, meaning 7 March, so she had to type 03/07. She almost missed it. "Arnab, is this right?" Her brother leaned over. "Looks fine. Submit." But the form also asked for a school code, and she didn't know it. Guessing felt dangerous. She messaged Mrs Ghosh, the olympiad teacher, and waited, jiggling her knee. Twenty minutes later the reply came with the code. Arohi checked the whole page once more against her ID, pressed Submit, and breathed out properly for the first time that evening.

qa.q: Who did Arohi message about the school code?
qa.a: Mrs Ghosh, the olympiad teacher.

qa.q: How was Arohi feeling while she filled in the form?
qa.a: She was anxious, her stomach knotted by the red warning, and she stayed tense, jiggling her knee, until she finally breathed out after submitting.

qa.q: Which of Arohi's steps protected her from a mistake she couldn't fix?
qa.a: Checking every letter against her school ID, catching the month-first date, and asking Mrs Ghosh for the code instead of guessing.

qa.q: How does Arnab see the form compared with Arohi?
qa.a: Arnab is relaxed and casual, happy to say "Submit", while Arohi feels how hard a wrong detail would be to correct.

grounding: Shows a teenager anxious about errors on an important form who reads carefully, checks against her ID and asks before submitting.
